subject: Cold War
overview: After World War II the United States and the Soviet Union, wartime allies, became rivals in a decades-long struggle between capitalism and communism that spread over almost the whole planet. They never fought each other directly. Instead they built nuclear arsenals that could destroy the world, raced each other into space, formed opposing alliances in NATO and the Warsaw Pact, and backed opposite sides in wars from Korea to Vietnam to Afghanistan. It ended without a final battle: the Eastern Bloc broke apart in 1989, and the Soviet Union itself was dissolved in December 1991.

key_moments.title: Berlin cut off, then supplied from the sky
key_moments.text: In June 1948 the **Soviet Union blocked all road, rail and canal access** to the American, British and French sectors of Berlin, a city deep inside the Soviet occupation zone of Germany. Rather than give up the city or force their way through, the Western Allies began the **Berlin Airlift**, flying in food, coal and medicine for about two million people. The planes kept coming for almost a year, until **Moscow lifted the blockade in May 1949**. Among the pilots was the American **Gail Halvorsen**, who dropped sweets on tiny handkerchief parachutes to the city's children and became known as the "Candy Bomber".
claims: The Soviet Union blockaded the Western sectors of Berlin beginning in June 1948.
The Western Allies supplied West Berlin by air during the Berlin Airlift.
The Soviet Union lifted the Berlin Blockade in May 1949.
American pilot Gail Halvorsen dropped candy on small parachutes to children in Berlin and was nicknamed the Candy Bomber.

key_moments.title: Sputnik starts the Space Race
key_moments.text: The Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, the **first artificial satellite**, a polished metal ball with four long antennas that circled the Earth and sent out a simple radio beep anyone with a receiver could pick up. The beep was a shock in the United States: a rocket that could put a satellite in orbit could also carry a nuclear warhead across the world. Washington responded by founding **NASA** in 1958, and the **Space Race** that followed ran through Yuri Gagarin's flight in 1961 to the **Apollo 11 Moon landing** in 1969. A satellite smaller than a beach ball ended up reshaping American schools and science funding for a generation.
claims: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957.
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite.
Sputnik 1 transmitted radio signals that could be received on Earth by amateur radio operators.
NASA was established in 1958, in response to the launch of Sputnik 1.
Apollo 11 landed astronauts on the Moon in 1969.

key_moments.title: Thirteen days on the nuclear brink
key_moments.text: American spy planes photographed **Soviet nuclear missile sites under construction in Cuba**, about 150 km from Florida. **President John F. Kennedy** ordered a naval "quarantine" around the island, and for about two weeks he and Soviet leader **Nikita Khrushchev** traded messages while their forces stood ready for war. The crisis ended when **the Soviets agreed to remove the missiles** in return for a public US promise not to invade Cuba and a secret deal to take American Jupiter missiles out of Turkey. Having come so close to disaster, both sides set up a **direct hotline** between Washington and Moscow in 1963.
claims: In October 1962 American U-2 reconnaissance flights photographed Soviet missile sites under construction in Cuba.
John F. Kennedy ordered a naval quarantine of Cuba during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
Nikita Khrushchev agreed to withdraw Soviet missiles from Cuba in exchange for a US public pledge not to invade Cuba.
The United States secretly agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey as part of the settlement of the Cuban Missile Crisis.
The Moscow–Washington hotline was established in 1963 after the Cuban Missile Crisis.

key_moments.title: The Wall opens and the Soviet Union ends
key_moments.text: Through 1989 communist governments across Eastern Europe fell one after another, mostly without bloodshed, as **Mikhail Gorbachev** declined to send Soviet troops to prop them up. On the evening of **9 November 1989**, East German official **Günter Schabowski** told a press conference that new travel rules took effect immediately, a mistake that sent crowds to the border until guards opened the gates of the **Berlin Wall**. Germany was **reunified in October 1990**. On **25 December 1991** Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin; the superpower at the center of the Cold War simply ceased to exist.
claims: Communist governments in several Eastern European countries fell during the Revolutions of 1989.
The Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989.
Günter Schabowski announced at a press conference on 9 November 1989 that new East German travel rules took effect immediately.
Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990.
Mikhail Gorbachev resigned as president of the Soviet Union on 25 December 1991.

deep_facts.text: The name of the conflict came from a writer before it had properly begun. In an essay of October 1945 called "You and the Atomic Bomb", George Orwell imagined a world split between a few superstates that could not conquer each other and would live in a permanent "cold war". The phrase entered American politics in 1947, when the financier Bernard Baruch used it in a speech, and it became common after the journalist Walter Lippmann made it the title of a book that same year. The author of Nineteen Eighty-Four thus named the standoff that would shape the next 44 years.
claims: George Orwell used the term cold war in his 1945 essay You and the Atomic Bomb.
Bernard Baruch used the term Cold War in a speech in 1947.
Walter Lippmann published a book titled The Cold War in 1947.

deep_facts.text: Shortly after midnight on 26 September 1983, at a time of high tension between the superpowers, the alarms went off in a command bunker near Moscow: the Soviet early-warning satellites reported that the United States had launched intercontinental missiles. The officer on duty, Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov, reasoned that a real American first strike would involve hundreds of missiles, not a handful, and reported a system malfunction instead of an attack. He was right. The satellites had mistaken sunlight reflecting off high clouds for rocket launches. Petrov received no award at the time, and the story stayed secret until after the Soviet Union had collapsed.
claims: On 26 September 1983 the Soviet early-warning system falsely reported launches of American intercontinental ballistic missiles.
Stanislav Petrov, the duty officer, judged the warning to be a false alarm and did not report it as an attack.
The 1983 false alarm was caused by sunlight reflecting off high-altitude clouds, which the satellites misread as missile launches.
The 1983 Soviet nuclear false alarm incident became publicly known only in the 1990s.

deep_facts.text: One of the most famous arguments of the Cold War took place beside a washing machine. In July 1959, at the American National Exhibition in Moscow, US Vice President Richard Nixon and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev stood in a model suburban kitchen and debated which system did more for ordinary people. Nixon praised American appliances, and Khrushchev answered that Soviet homes would soon have all of them too. The "Kitchen Debate" was shown on television in both countries, and it turned the rivalry between two nuclear powers, for one afternoon, into an argument over consumer goods.
claims: The Kitchen Debate took place in July 1959 at the American National Exhibition in Moscow.
The Kitchen Debate was between US Vice President Richard Nixon and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev.
Part of the Kitchen Debate took place in a model American kitchen at the exhibition.
The Kitchen Debate was broadcast on television in both the United States and the Soviet Union.

connections.name: Joseph Stalin
connections.connection: Led the Soviet Union into the Cold War, installing communist governments across Eastern Europe and ordering the 1948 Berlin Blockade.

connections.name: Harry S. Truman
connections.connection: Set the US policy of containing communism with the Truman Doctrine in 1947 and ordered the Berlin Airlift.

connections.name: Nikita Khrushchev
connections.connection: Soviet leader who placed nuclear missiles in Cuba in 1962 and then agreed to withdraw them.

connections.name: John F. Kennedy
connections.connection: US president who ordered the naval quarantine of Cuba during the 1962 missile crisis.

connections.name: Mikhail Gorbachev
connections.connection: Last Soviet leader, whose reforms and refusal to crush the 1989 revolutions led to the end of the Cold War.

connections.name: Ronald Reagan
connections.connection: US president who built up the military in the 1980s and later signed the 1987 INF Treaty with Gorbachev.

connections.name: World War II
connections.connection: Left the United States and the Soviet Union as the two dominant powers, with Europe divided between their armies.

connections.name: Korean War
connections.connection: The first major armed conflict of the Cold War, with US-led UN forces against North Korea and China from 1950 to 1953.

connections.name: Vietnam War
connections.connection: A long proxy war in which the United States backed South Vietnam while the Soviet Union and China supported North Vietnam.

connections.name: Cuban Missile Crisis
connections.connection: The October 1962 standoff over Soviet missiles in Cuba, the closest the Cold War came to nuclear war.

connections.name: Space Race
connections.connection: The superpowers' competition in spaceflight, from Sputnik 1 in 1957 to the Apollo Moon landings.

connections.name: Revolutions of 1989
connections.connection: The wave of uprisings that brought down the communist governments of Eastern Europe, including the opening of the Berlin Wall.

connections.name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
connections.connection: The breakup of the Soviet Union in December 1991 that ended the Cold War.

connections.name: Soviet–Afghan War
connections.connection: The Soviet intervention in Afghanistan from 1979 to 1989, in which the United States armed the mujahideen opposing it.
